display_title_he: התמודדות עם טראומה של אלימות במשפחה
short_summary: A woman whose mother was killed by a partner when she was a toddler is speaking out about domestic abuse after discovering the full details of the tragedy at age 18.

image.credit: U.S. Department of State · Public domain

sources.name: BBC News
sources.title: Daughter of woman killed by partner 'refuses to be another victim'

paragraphs: When Keeley McKee was just a toddler, her life was permanently altered by domestic violence. In March 2003, weeks before she was scheduled to marry her partner, her mother Leanne McKee was killed by him, and the perpetrator subsequently took his own life. On the fatal night of the tragedy, Keeley was staying safely with her grandmother, anticipating that her mother would collect her the following day. Protected by her relatives as she grew up, she remained largely unaware of the exact, brutal circumstances surrounding her mother's death. Nevertheless, early childhood memories lingered, including a frightening instance when her mother told her to hide in a bedroom and not come out until called, while someone attempted to force entry.

It was not until Keeley reached her eighteenth birthday that the stark reality of the past finally came to light. Driven by an underlying intuition, she searched online and unexpectedly discovered a news article detailing the murder, reading about the event in the most brutal way imaginable. Confronting the truth in such an abrupt manner sent her into a severe downward spiral. She admitted that she had previously been in denial, choosing not to face or believe what she subconsciously suspected, and reading the report caused her to run away entirely from the grieving process. Overwhelmed by deep anger, confusion, and unmanaged trauma, her mental health deteriorated rapidly. She withdrew from family and friends, suffered from suicidal ideation, attempted to take her own life on multiple occasions, and struggled extensively with drug and alcohol misuse.

Furthermore, the trauma deeply affected her perception of love and relationships. She lived in constant fear of abandonment, afraid to fully love in case that affection would be abruptly taken away again, and found it difficult to trust others. Despite these profound relational hurdles, she maintains that she still has much love to give and firmly believes that the right day will come when she can build a strong family unit. Participating in a Christian discipleship programme and leaning on her faith ultimately provided her with the emotional fuel, fight, and courage to confront the past rather than continually running from it. Embracing a resolute mindset, she decided to transform her painful experiences into an active stand against domestic abuse.

Today, Keeley channels her grief into raising awareness about the devastating, long-lasting consequences that domestic abuse inflicts upon children and families left behind, who are often left struggling with unaddressed trauma. Raised lovingly by her great-aunt and great-uncle while they navigated their own profound period of mourning for Leanne, she understands the vital importance of a supportive environment. She emphasizes that violence has unfortunately become normalized in society and that much more must be done to tackle it. Refusing to be just another victim of this story, she urges people currently experiencing abusive relationships to consider both their own futures and the psychological impact on their children, warning that children raised in such environments may normalize the behavior and potentially treat their future partners the same way.

facts.fact: Keeley McKee was three years old when her mother Leanne was killed by her partner in March 2003.
Keeley only learned the full details of her mother's murder when she turned 18 by finding an online news report.
Following the discovery, Keeley's mental health deteriorated, leading to substance abuse, isolation, and suicide attempts.
Keeley credits a Christian discipleship programme and her faith with helping her confront her past and refuse to remain a victim.
She was raised by her great-aunt and great-uncle and now campaigns to highlight domestic abuse and its long-term impact on families.
